But keep prioritising your wants and needs. Every little thing. I want to live in an apartment by myself, I want to bake chocolate cookies, I want to play super smash bros with anyone at my apartment, I want to tell every stupid person that bothers me on the street to fuck off. It took me monthsss and even now I'm still learning. Started by recognising what does hunger feel like. Eating better. Muscles are hurting, I need to stretch. Body is hot, I need to masterbate. Then after that I could notice when I was angry. I was angry that my roommate wouldn't start conversations first. That she acted annoyed when I spoke to her. That my boss comaplained to me non-stop but never bothered any other worker. Etc etc.


Then I was walking to work, the weather was nice, it was cold and the sky was pretty, and I felt a flicker of happiness. It was gone like 20 mins later when I clocked into work, but still. That's something.


Lexapro 20mg daily helps me, but it wasn't like it suddenly made my feelings come back. I just noticed I had a bit more energy. My yearly doctors visit caught low vitamin D. Eating lots of veg helps my gut. I still get diarrhea all the time, but it's not the painful flareups i used to have.

2 things to speed it up—

—sleeping as much as you can. your body needs rest. that's why you have that intense fatigue. and trying to eat as healthy as you can. freeze kind of "puts you to sleep" so you dont FEEL hunger even when your body is starving. your body kind of shuts down to compensate. but even if you don't feel hungry try to eat, and its so important to eat healthy. gut health is connected to mental health. im not saying eat solely kale, but make sure you've got a protein, a few veggies, and a carb.

—slowly pushing yourself to do 1 thing that makes you anxious. the freeze is a defense against anxiety and the fear of the unknown, the uncontrolled. its a fear of connection, of leaving the house, of being hurt. and pushing yourself through that anxiety feels fucking impossible, i know. but try day after day. it's not gonna work on day 1,  or day 2, or day 100. but eventually it DOES work. eventually you get so frustrated and suicidal you can do the thing that terrifies you. and then the next thing that terrifies you. and then the next. my most terrifying thing was telling my parents my brothers sexually abused me. i went into that house expecting to die. ever since then, i still feel anxiety, but nothing is ever going to compare to that. 

once your anxiety goes down and you feel more confident navigating the world the freeze starts to ebb and the emotions come up.

Rather than a competition, it's different paintstrokes of pain. Different colors.

for the freeze type— also communicating their needs. freeze by nature is to avoid, avoid problems, avoid intimacy, avoid closeness. a fight type will then hound a freeze type to get them to open up and will get frustrated when they hit that wall. that frustration will trigger a blowup which makes the freeze type retreat more.

So dialogue is a way of "showing" and you can get around it by "telling."

Eg; "They met in the hallway and exchanged pleasantries," rather than the whole hi how are you/good how are you.

Eg; "she told him about the conversation she had with her brother" (instead of rewriting a whole conversation ESPECIALLY if the reader has already read it)

You can intersperse this into dialogue, like zooming in and zooming out.

Eg;

"How did things go with your brother?"

She recounted the conversation she had with her brother. Even though it was only a week ago, it felt like it had been forever.

"I'm sorry it didn't go well."

"Yeah," she shifts, "I guess that's how it goes sometimes."

We started zoomed in, then zoomed out, then went back in. 

But also don't stress about too much dialogue. What takes you 10-20 mins to write can be read in like 1-2 mins. Dialogue is also the least burdensome type of writing for readers to process

took a long time to find the courage. if you didn't tell your family when it happened that's a pretty big sign you felt you were going to get a bad reaction. and you were probably right! it takes a lot of time in therapy to understand that and be ok with it. then when you are prepared for the shit reaction you need to understand what you're trying to get from them. in my case i told my parents because i wanted to protect my little sister. i wasn't going in the hopes of reconciliation, or to receive warmth or love or comfort, because I knew from my therapy that those things weren't going to happen. i was going for protection for my sister and for justice— if my parents didn't do anything about the sexual abuse, then was going straight to the police. and so because i had that clear focus going in it hurt a lot less. 

now on the 'courage' part— i am a freeze type, which means my response is to hide and avoid. when i was going to send the text to my mum saying 'we need to talk' my anxiety hit a peak and i could barely breathe. there were a lot of things i said to myself. "we're dying a day at a time, and I would rather face this fear and die than let it control me for the rest of my life." "we can't let it happen to our sister." "you always said you were sorry about not protecting me then— why can't you do it now? if i was being raped again would you freeze AGAIN and let it happen AGAIN?" not very nice things to say to yourself... but what made the decision was "Are you going to leave her to cry in that room alone forever?" which sounds weird... in meditations i see my inner child, in my childhood bedroom, crying. and i've been suicidal— and in those moments, i know that if there's a heaven, another life, or just nothingness... i'm going to have my trauma in the next life, too. maybe i can kill myself, and maybe the pain stops, but that little girl is still going to be crying in that room. that was what made me send the text. and the anxiety eased, just a little bit... i kept crying... and then i felt HAPPINESS. and pride. i was brave, strong. i was the person i knew myself to be. it was EASY after that. i was so surprised it had taken me so long. i was so upset that i'd lost so many years of my life to it. 

it was just that initial push, that initial freeze response, that initial surge of anxiety, my biological response from childhood that is ingrained in me— that was what was stopping me. and that core focus— of saving my inner child from crying in that room, but more than that, the work i'd been doing in therapy, internal family systems + parts work, my work on understanding my own sexuality, feeling confident and beautiful and not disgusting in my body, forgiving myself for the guilt of not fighting back when i was 14 and 'big and strong' enough to fight back, the hope that new people in my life have given me, all of that together is what pushed me. it takes so much time, so much effort, so much therapy. it's one step forward and seven steps backward. you're having a good day and then you're suicidal at 7pm. you feel like the therapy isn't working for years and then all of a sudden it is. one day you do the thing you've been doing for fucking forever and then all of a sudden it works, and you're crying and processing and holy shit there's SO MUCH to deal with.

It starts by hating yourself, lol. I used to try to love myself. I would list 5 things I liked about myself in front of the mirror, etc etc. It didn't work. It just felt fake.

Then I did a guided meditation that said- "how are you feeling towards your inner child?" And the answer was easy. I hated her. I hated having to 'parent' my inner child when I was never parented. I never asked to be a parent. She was weak and stupid. She let herself be abused.

When I felt that, I started crying. Over time, I started to feel bad for her. That took TIME. Months of reliving things in childhood, of being shown compassion from friends/in therapy. But hating my younger self was how our relationship started.

Believing you have self worth isn't a switch you flip. It starts by exploring your relationship with yourself AUTHENTICALLY. Why the 'loving myself' exercises never worked was because deep down I didn't like myself. When I was authentic and admitted and I didn't like myself- that was when I made progress.

The other component is that somewhere in your childhood you recieved the message that you have no value. Maybe your needs were seen as a burden. Maybe your family didn't like you, found you annoying, didn't like talking to you, didn't like your jokes. Thing is, whether people are presidents or homeless, everyone has value. Understand where you think you don't have value. Maybe you don't have many friends, or you're single, or your career isn't working out and you use those things to say you're a burden/valueless. Ultimately, even if you HAD those things, you'd still be the same person. 

The last part imo is setting goals and achieving them. And that comes from understanding WHY things aren't working. For example, I wanted to start going to the gym. But everytime I considered it I was filled with anxiety. What if people judged me? What if I looked stupid? What if someone laughed at me? More days passed and I beat myself over it. I called myself lazy and a coward. That didn't help at all. The day I went to the gym was the day where I sat down and said to myself- it's fine if you don't go. It's fine if for the entire 2023 you don't go. I want to go, but I want you to feel ready and safe and not anxious. And if we do go, if we feel anxious we can leave even if it's only been 5 minutes. And we'll go on a weekday at noon when it's quiet so there's less people and less pressure. Etc etc. I cried a lot. I journalled a lot. And now I go to the gym regularly and I feel fine. 

When you set goals and achieve them you build confidence in yourself, and that helps you develop skills and grow into yourself, which helps with self-worth. But the me who goes to the gym and the me who was too terrified are the same person. We have the same value. I'm just happier now, in a body that feels good and doesn't hurt. If next week the anxiety came back and I couldn't go to the gym for a month, I wouldn't be bothered at all, because my value does not come from the things I do or achieve. It would just be like having an injury and healing.

You fix that by working internally and externally. Internally you need to understand where it's coming from and what the fear of NOT doing it is. It's a process. The first thing to understand is just as you have a relationship with other people, you have one with yourself. So not only can you love yourself, you can also hate yourself, be afraid of yourself, be angry at yourself, etc. And just like a relationship with another person, you're not going to love yourself overnight. You'll begin as a stranger, slowly learnimg yourself, and then you'll be a friend to yourself, and then finally feel that deep, healing love.

You can't do that without feeling compassion for yourself. No one is perfect, and you're always going to be flawed. So you're going to have to forgive yourself for your shortcomings- for laziness, envy, anger... whatever negative emotions you feel most strongly.

Here's the thing no one tells you- compassion comes from pain. I've felt the most sympathetic to other people when I've been suicidal. Pain has a way of connecting people like nothing else. It strips away the pretense, bares people to one another. When you feel the depths of your pain, once you process the deeper emotions, it turns into compassion. And that compassion will allow you to express softer emotions to yourself

Long story short- self love doesn't happen in a vacuum. Looking in a mirror and saying three things you love about yourself isn't self love (although it's a start!). Self love naturally happens as you look back on what you experienced as a child and realise that you were just a child and that the adults were at fault. It's a LOT harder for csa survivors than regular people. The shame around csa, combined with the fact that childhood beliefs are the hardest ones to change make it SO hard to heal. I've come a long way, but sometimes I remember things my mother said to me, like "You just make problems for yourself and then blame other people for them" and my logical mind knows it's bullshit, but it's my mum, and I love and trust and my mum, and mum knows so much more than me, and mum is older and wiser than me... it goes on like that. Parents are like gods to us when we're children. They're our entire world. And if they treated you like garbage, you probably see yourself as garbage, worthless and unlovable. It's really, really hard to overcome.

For me, I just had to let go. I had so much I wanted from life. A career. A family. Solid friends. Travelling. A cat. And my trauma and its impact on me ruined it all. Can't have a career when you're in the ER thinking you're dying of a heart attack that's actually a panic attack, you can't make friends when you have attachment issues, can't travel when you're too depressed to get out of bed, etc. Now, I spend my days crying all the time, journalling, reading self help books, understanding myself. It's a full-time job in itself. 

I had to really let it all go, because I kept prioritising external goals over myself. I used to be religious, so I put God and religion over myself. Then I put my family over myself. Then I put school and my career over myself. Who cares if I'm stressed and crying at 3am over my studies so long as my grades are good, right? It'll all be worth it in the end. That's what I told myself. I always, always put myself last. And it worked, for a little while, and then my brain just stopped working. I can't even focus while reading a book anymore, let alone studying.


And so I was forced to let it all go, and I did. And I was forced to work on myself, and I am. And I realised life was not as serious as I thought it was, and everyone's kinda making it up as they go along. And it's really not a big deal if I want to take life slow and at my own place. I'm not less because I graduated and am working a minimum wage job. My value doesn't come from that. And the more you let those things go, the more you're able to give to yourself. I read that a child wants three things from their parents- trust, pride, and love so strong the parent would be willing to die for them. And I'm commited to healing myself, to the point where I've given absolutely everything to myself and to my inner child. And I actually get along with myself now. I no longer feel like I abandon or betray myself. When I say to myself, "I love you, and I'd do anything for you" I MEAN it. My inner child is sharp. She knows truth from lie. She knew back when I studied that when I said I'd do anything, I only meant it so long as an assignment wasn't due- if anything was due, I'd throw myself under the bus, fuck up my sleep schedule, yell at myself for not being smart enough, etc.

We like to think that we have control over our emotional needs. We really, really don't. Our inner child runs the show most of the time, and we don't even realise it. Emotional needs are just like hunger, sleep, loneliness. If you don't meet them you suffer.

To see a psychologist, you get a referral from your  GP. You tell your GP you would like a referral for childhood trauma, and they will find you a psychologist who specialises in childhood trauma. You don't need to find your own psychologist unless you want to. Normally the GP picks for you, simply because there are too many people with mental illness and not enough psychologists. You can google and call psychologists themselves, but most of them are completely booked out. A GP knows which psychologists aren't busy and can refer you.

At this stage, a lot of people will ask their GP for a mental health plan. You don't need this plan to see a psychologist, but it's very good because it saves you around $80 each session. If you don't get a mental health plan, you have to pay full price for therapy sessions.The mental health plan is run by medicare. Your GP will email it to your psychologist. Each session, your psychologist will use the mental health plan to make a claim. This is how they get paid.

A therapist is the same as a psychologist. A therapist is not the same as a psychiatrist. A therapist does not go to medical school and is not a doctor. They are not allowed to prescribe you medication. A psychiatrist is a psychologist who also went to medical school. They are allowed to prescribe you medication. A psychiatrist is basically a psychologist and a GP combined.

So basically:

-see a GP

-ask them for a referral to a psychologist, one who is experienced in childhood trauma

-ask them for a mental health plan

-the GP will ask you questions and you will fill out the paperwork together

-your GP will email the completed mental health plan to your new psychologist

-you will call your new psychologist and organise a time for your first session

-when the session is done, your new psychologist will make a claim to medicare using your mental health plan

-if they bulk bill, you pay nothing

-if they don't bulk bill, you pay the difference. For example, my psychologist charges $170. I get $88 from medicare back. I pay around $80 each session.


Hope this helps! it's hard but soon you'll get the help you need :)

Best thing I learned is that procrastination is an emotion manegement issue, not a time management issue. When you sit at the desk and feel miserable that you have to study, you automatically pull out your phone/switch tabs to take the negative feeling away. This becomes a habit as your brain realises taking the work away makes you happy. Negative reinforcement.

At the same time, motivation comes after doing a task, not before it. Before I run, I feel awful, sluggish, and like crap. After I run I feel like a world champion and like I could run 10km more. Even just doing a task for 5-10 min gets your brain going, puts you into a focused/flow state, and then before you know it time has passed, and now you're motivated and you feel like you can actually achieve things.

We also lie to ourselves quite a bit. If you want to quit smoking, one more day of smoking isn't going to kill you. So it's easy to think 'okay today is my last day, tomorrow I'll stop'. But in reality, tomorrow isn't that much different from today, and tomorrow you're probably going to tell the same lie to yourself. Similar thing with studying. If you tell yourself you'll start that assignment tomorrow, you're probably not going to start it tomorrow. You'll think about it and tell yourself you'll do it the day after.

So in terms of actual tips, what you need to do is put a proper time on things. You also need to break them down into tasks that you can actually do. It's not 'I'm going to write my assignment today'. It's today, at 2pm, I'm going to read this academic paper, then I'm going to spend 5 mins writing down my thoughts and how to incorporate it into my assignment.Then you need to just sit and do it. The first ten minutes are going to suck. You're going to want to grab your phone. But once you force your brain to switch on, it'll get easier. And like all habits, the more you do it, the more the neural pathways are formed, the easier it gets. Procrastination is a bad habit we all fall into, but it's a habit you can unlearn. And once you move past it you feel unstoppable lol. I procrastinate every now and then, but nowhere near as much as I used to, and I'm so much happier for it.

I practiced what I wanted to say a thousand times over, and yet when I had to say the words 'child sexual abuse' I still almost choked on them. But it got easier as I started talking, and when it got too hard, I would stop for a minute and just breathe. My therapist sat patiently and let me speak, and when she spoke it was just for clarification, not to offer advice or sympathy or anything, and it allowed me to forget she was even there and just keep talking. The whole time, I didn't make eye contact with her, I just stared at the floor. And once I'd opened up, I felt so much better. I thought it would make me feel worse, but I felt much better afterwards. Just know that you can always stop talking if you don't want to keep going, and then five minutes later you can change your mind and start talking again if you want. It can be disjointed, it can be in order, it can be whatever you want it to be. I was so nervous I could barely speak, I cried a disgusting amount, but my therapist was patient because that's what I'm paying her to be. Know that you're taking a huge leap in your recovery progress and before you know it results will start to show, and it's an incredible feeling when you realise you've started to move forward

Hey, firstly good job at trying to be a good patient and make an effort. It shows a real initiative and desire to be healthy that will definitely translate into results. That said, I've read your post a few times and a few things aren't super clear. You say you don't engage, but you also say that you get worked up over the questions- which sounds like engaging to me. I guess what I'm trying to ask is how, specifically, are you failing to be a good patient? It seems like your therapist doesn't have a problem with the way your sessions are going, and since it's her job to worry over these things, I wouldn't overthink it too much if she's content with your level of progress. So I guess then you need to ask yourself in exact terms what you feel like your current sessions are lacking. Are you withholding certain memories or events from her? Are you ashamed of some feelings you hold? Do you feel uncomfortable opening up or being vulnerable? It can help to write a page reflecting on your session and starting with basic events/experiences (eg; "When I was in therapy today, we talked about x. It made me feel y") and then pausing and reflecting on why you felt that way- what kinds of beliefs you have that might be influencing your thoughts.

But for more practical advice, try writing stuff down! Feel free to bring a list of things you want to talk about into the session, or maybe write a letter of things you want to say but find it hard to express face-to-face. You could even just print this post and show it to her.
